text:
This guide is for UK-qualified professionals and businesses who want to understand how to get their UK professional qualifications recognised internationally (including in North, Central and Latin America, Africa, Middle East, Asia, Australia, New Zealand and wider Europe).

For guidance on providing services in the EU, read ‘Recognition of UK professional qualifications in EU member states’. Recognition requirements and processes vary by country and by profession.

This guidance explains the typical steps, where to find authoritative information, and what to prepare before you contact the relevant overseas regulator or competent authority.

Overview

What recognition means

Some professions are regulated in law. This means there is a legal requirement to have your professional qualifications (and sometimes your experience) assessed before you can carry out certain professional activities or use a protected professional title, like ‘architect’.

In most countries, recognition decisions are made by the overseas regulator or ‘competent authority’ for that profession. There is no single international system for recognition, so you will usually need to check requirements for your specific profession and the country (or region) where you want to work. You may also need to meet separate requirements for registration and licensure, such as visas or work permits.

This guidance is focused on recognition of professional qualifications (RPQ) and does not replace advice from overseas regulators, employers or immigration authorities.

Before you start:

confirm the country where you want to work. If the country has a federalised regulation system (for example, some licensing is set at state or provincial level), be prepared to check rules for the specific state, province, territory or region where you will work

be clear about the professional activities you want to carry out and the title you want to use

confirm whether you will provide services temporarily, occasionally, or on a long-term basis (requirements can differ)

gather evidence of your UK qualifications, your UK professional registration, your work experience and qualifications from the relevant UK competent authority or chartered/professional membership body – you may need to provide copies of these to confirm your qualifications and registration status

allow time and budget for fees, translations, certification of documents and (in some cases) tests or adaptation periods

check whether you need to meet language requirements

Step 1: check whether your profession is regulated in your target country

Not every profession is regulated in every country. In some places you can work without having your qualification formally recognised, but you may still need to meet other requirements (for example, visa/work requirements, employer checks, licensing rules, or membership of a professional body).

Check:

the target country’s government websites for information on regulated professions and licensing

websites of the overseas regulator or professional body for your profession

If the country has multiple jurisdictions (for example, federal systems), check requirements for the specific state, province or region.

Trade associations, chambers of commerce and employers may be able to point you to the correct regulator, but you should still verify requirements with the regulator directly.

Step 2: identify the overseas regulator or competent authority

If your profession is regulated, you will usually need to apply to the overseas regulator or competent authority to have your qualifications assessed. In some countries, there may be different bodies for registration, licensing, and professional conduct.

In countries with federal or devolved systems, regulation can be set at state, provincial or territorial level. This can mean there is more than one competent authority, depending on where you plan to work.

When you contact the overseas regulator, ask what you need to do to practise your profession in that country.

For example, ask about:

whether your UK qualifications are eligible for assessment

the application route (for example, for experienced professionals, new graduates, or temporary services)

documents you must provide (and whether they must be certified or translated)

fees and expected processing times

any exams, interviews, supervised practice or adaptation periods

language requirements

how to appeal or request a review if your application is refused

Step 3: check whether any recognition arrangement is available

In some cases, there may be bilateral recognition arrangements that make it easier to have your UK qualification recognised overseas. These can include Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) between regulatory or professional bodies, or other arrangements such as memoranda of understanding (MoUs).

Some UK trade agreements include frameworks to support recognition discussions between regulators, but recognition decisions are still made by the overseas regulator. You should check with the regulator what, if any, arrangement applies to your profession. See Annex 1 for a select list of arrangements that UK regulated sectors have with international partners, and Annex 2 for a list of broader country-level agreements.

You can also read ‘Arrangements to facilitate the recognition of professional qualifications’ for background on different types of arrangements.

Step 4: prepare your evidence and apply

Most regulators will have an application process for overseas-qualified professionals. You may need to apply online, pay a fee, and provide documents to show your identity, qualifications and professional experience.

Common documents can include:

your passport or other identity documents

qualification certificates and transcripts

evidence of professional registration or membership in the UK (if applicable)

references, employment history, or evidence of practice hours

evidence of professional indemnity insurance (for some professions)

criminal record or fitness to practise checks (for some professions)

certified translations, if required

Common requirements and things to prepare for

Countries with state, provincial or territorial regulation

If regulation is set at state, provincial or territorial level, you may need to repeat steps 1 to 4 for the specific jurisdiction where you will work. Ask whether the regulator recognises your qualification for that jurisdiction, and whether you can transfer recognition if you later move within the country.

Fees and timescales

Costs and processing times vary widely. As well as application fees, you may need to budget for translations, certification of documents, travel, and any tests or courses required by the regulator.

Language requirements

Some regulators require evidence of language proficiency, especially where you will have direct contact with the public. Requirements can include formal tests or evidence of professional experience in the language.

Tests, interviews or supervised practice

If the regulator identifies differences between your UK qualification and the local requirements, you may need to do one of the following:

take an aptitude test

complete an interview

complete an online learning module

undertake a period of supervised practice or adaptation

Translating and certifying documents

You may need to provide certified copies and certified translations of your documents. Some countries also require documents to be authenticated (for example, using an apostille). Check the regulator’s guidance before you pay for translations or certification.

If you cannot get recognition

If you cannot get your qualification recognised, or the process would take too long, you may have other options depending on your profession and target market.

For example:

ask the regulator whether there are alternative routes (such as, an assessment based on professional experience)

consider roles where recognition is not required, or where you work under supervision

consider completing any additional training, tests or local qualifications needed

ask the regulator about review or appeal processes if your application is refused

Get help and related guidance

Start with the overseas regulator or competent authority for your profession, as they can tell you the correct route and requirements.

Use the UK Regulated Professions Register to check whether your profession is regulated in the UK and who the UK regulator is.

If you are providing professional services overseas (for example, as a self-employed professional or through your employer), business.gov.uk has export support guidance on recognition of professional qualifications and how to get help from the export support team.

For background on recognition arrangements, read ‘Arrangements to facilitate the recognition of professional qualifications’.

If you are providing services in the EU, read ‘Recognition of UK professional qualifications in EU member states’.

This guidance provides general information. If you spot something that is out of date, choose the ‘Report a problem with this page’ button at the end of this GOV.UK webpage.

Annex 1: a select list of arrangements that UK regulated sectors have with international partners

Wording index

The following are descriptions of types of agreements but titling may vary in the agreements themselves.

Bilateral accreditation arrangement

This provides recognition of qualifications from specific accredited education providers or programmes, rather than reciprocal recognition between regulatory bodies.

Direct Membership Agreement (one way)

This provides a one-way membership route for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and local licensing requirements may still apply.

Direct route to membership

This provides a direct route to membership for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and additional local requirements may apply.

Memorandum of understanding (MoU)

This provides a framework for co-operation, information sharing, recognition discussions, or pathways between organisations. It does not automatically confer practising rights or recognition unless explicitly stated.

Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA)

A formal agreement between 2 or more parties (usually regulatory bodies) which aims to facilitate mobility of professionals through agreed mutual recognition, registration or membership processes. Subject to agreed criteria and local requirements.

Mutual Recognition of Professional Qualifications (MRPQ)

This provides reciprocal recognition of professional qualifications between participating bodies, subject to any specified eligibility criteria and local requirements.

Pathway to membership/study route

This provides a route to body membership through examinations, additional study, experience requirements or other prescribed criteria. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred.

Reciprocal Membership Agreement

This provides a reciprocal membership route for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and local licensing requirements may still apply.

Recognition / practice route

This provides a route to recognition for practice in the overseas jurisdiction, subject to local conditions.

Regulatory co-operation

This provides a regulatory co-operation framework. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred.

Unilateral Recognition Agreement

This rovides a one-way route for eligible professionals from one jurisdiction to have their qualification, registration or membership recognised by another body. It is not automatically reciprocal, so professionals moving the other way may need to use a different route.

This list is not exhaustive and is subject to change. For further information, refer to the relevant authority/professional/regulatory bodies’ websites.
